Task completion times for correct answers were significantly faster for the cartesian layout.

Waldner et al. [54] found that length and position channels make it easier to identify and compare visual representations in linear layouts. This study recommends linear layouts when length and position are used in the encoding component for identifying and comparing tasks.
A vertical cursor line and row numbers were shown only for the linear condition. The cursor in the linear layout did not affect the performance much.
Circular layouts largely rely on manual design, limiting their efficiency and general applicability.

There are no use cases for aligning tracks with different lengths. A common limitation of existing tools is the lack of support for both linear and circular layouts. The utility of space-filling and 3D layouts in the context of a grammar is limited as they do not afford alignment with other tracks.

Circular layouts offer compactness and multidimensional representation capabilities. The rendering logic is kept lightweight and invokes modular components to assemble multilayered circular layouts. We aim to extend support beyond circular layouts.

There is evidence that circular layouts are preferable in some cases. Circular graph layouts can be attractive for visualization designers. Bending the main axis into a circular shape is convenient for fitting long data sequences into a quadratic space.
The report hinted at the benefit of adopting the circular layout for application to structural data.

Performance of an area estimation task has been shown to be similar for circles and rectangles. The results indicated that it is easier to remember positions in a radial coordinate system than a cartesian one. Empirical evidence is provided for the suitability of linear and circular layouts for two data types.

Participants reported they could not scan all rows from left to right in one go, but needed to vertically subdivide the graph. Vertically subdividing the graph made it more difficult to spot contamination events between samples on rows far apart. Staying on the same row or in the same column was cited as a major difficulty for the contamination detection task with a circular layout.
Circular tracks are not effective for tasks in which users have to focus on a local region, as discussed in the feedback from Scenario 1.

Visualization researchers generally advise against making visualizations with radial layouts. For comparisons of length and position, the authors conclude that circular layouts are not useful citing Waldner et al.

The mouse-over effect on the circular layout interactions visualization required holding down the Alt-key. For the linear layout, a majority of participants appeared to scan the visualization from left to right. Scanning from left to right was not observed as many times or as clearly for the circular layout.
